resident.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old man presented with neck pain of 6 months' duration, with paraesthesia radiating from both shoulders to the fingers, and worsening weakness in both lower extremities over 5 months.
resident.history: The patient had intermittent neck pain with paraesthesia in both shoulders radiating to the fingers, mostly during activities, for 6 months. There was no prior trauma. Over the following 5 months, the pain and paraesthesia worsened, and he developed weakness in both lower extremities. He consulted a neurosurgeon, who stated there was nerve entrapment. He underwent physiotherapy for 4 months without improvement. He then presented to our hospital. He worked as a contractor and mostly sat behind a desk. He denied any decrease in body weight or appetite and had no history of chronic cough.
resident.physical_exam: On physical examination, general condition was unremarkable (further details not documented). There was no tenderness on palpation along the midline. Examination of the cervical spine showed positive Lhermitte test, finger-escape test, grip-and-release test, Hoffman-Tromner sign, and Spurling sign. The patient was able to move his neck normally. Further examination revealed diminished motoric strength in all extremities with positive Babinski reflex and clonus, with normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes. He had urinary retention and faecal incontinence. Radiographic examination showed straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter of 10 mm and a Torg ratio of 0.37. There was osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 levels with spur formation at C3 through C5. Magnetic resonance imaging showed cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 levels and spinal cord compression. Laboratory findings were unremarkable except for leukocytosis.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy, plus a likely cervical radiculopathy (C5 or C6) suggested by radicular symptoms and a positive Spurling sign.

red_flags.finding: Positive Spurling sign with paresthesias radiating from shoulders to fingers
red_flags.rationale: Indicates a radicular component in addition to myelopathy. The MRI report describes canal stenosis and cord compression but does not mention foraminal stenosis; if present, decompression should address the nerve roots as well.

red_flags.finding: Normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes despite positive Babinski reflex and clonus
red_flags.rationale: Upper motor neuron lesions typically cause hyperreflexia. Normal DTRs may reflect early myelopathy or a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, but they do not undermine the evidence of cord compression.
Not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of the myelopathy. It may indicate an unrelated infection or inflammation but does not alter the localization or indication.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The MRI report describes central canal stenosis and cord compression at C4-C5, which explains the myelopathic syndrome. However, the radicular symptoms (shoulder-to-finger paresthesias, positive Spurling sign) are not directly explained by the reported imaging; foraminal stenosis is not described.

(2) Normal patellar and Achilles reflexes despite Babinski and clonus—coexisting—an atypical finding possibly due to early myelopathy or coexisting peripheral neuropathy; does not alter the main diagnosis. (3) Leukocytosis—coexisting—incidental laboratory abnormality not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of cord compression.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the progressive myelopathy and the evidence that delay may risk irreversible cord damage. However, the patient is only 50 years old and has not had a structured, supervised conservative program with clear goals and close monitoring. I propose a formal 3-6 month course of intensive physical therapy, core strengthening, posture management, and symptom control, with defined failure criteria. Success rates from structured conservative care in mild-to-moderate compressive myelopathy are around 30%, but in this case with severe myelopathy and already failed physiotherapy, that figure may be optimistic. Nevertheless, given the risks of surgery, a time-limited trial under strict supervision is a reasonable first step. If there is no improvement after 6 weeks or if neurological deficits worsen, I would accept surgery.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 50-year-old man with a 6-month history of progressive cervical myelopathy caused by C4-C5 spinal cord compression. Clinical findings include long-tract signs (Lhermitte, finger-escape, grip-and-release, Hoffman-Tromner, Babinski, clonus) and sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention, faecal incontinence), which are severe and indicate significant cord involvement. Four months of physiotherapy failed to halt progression. Imaging confirms canal stenosis with cord compression, though the direction of compression, degree of stenosis, T2 cord signal, and foraminal involvement are not documented. In my opinion, this is a surgical-grade myelopathy; continued delay risks irreversible spinal cord injury. However, further characterisation of the compression and clarification of the unexplained leukocytosis are prudent before finalising the surgical plan.
proposed_options: Early surgical decompression of C4-C5 via anterior approach (ACDF or ACCF) or posterior approach (laminectomy/laminoplasty) depending on detailed imaging and sagittal alignment, with or without fusion.

Obtain additional imaging (high-resolution MRI with T2 signal and foraminal sequences, thin-slice CT, dynamic flexion-extension radiographs) and infection workup for leukocytosis, then proceed to definitive decompression once anatomy and medical status are clarified.

Structured, time-limited supervised conservative trial (e.g., 6 weeks) with intensive physiotherapy, posture management, and strict neurological monitoring, with predefined failure criteria mandating surgical conversion if there is any deterioration or lack of improvement.
disagreement_points: I respectfully disagree with the rehabilitation physician's proposal for a 3-6 month conservative trial; in progressive myelopathy with sphincter involvement, further delay risks irreversible cord damage and may convert a potentially reversible situation into permanent disability.

The available MRI description lacks critical details (compression vector, T2 cord signal change, foraminal stenosis). These affect surgical approach and risk stratification and should be obtained before committing to a specific operative plan.
The unexplained leukocytosis requires evaluation before any elective surgery, as it may indicate an infectious or inflammatory process that could influence timing and perioperative management.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed to early surgery after a focused workup, or allow a structured short conservative trial under strict criteria?
If surgery is selected, which decompression approach (anterior vs posterior) do you consider most appropriate given the available imaging and sagittal alignment?
How urgent should we consider this case? Is surgery to be scheduled within days, or is a short delay for additional imaging and infection workup acceptable?
Do you want to obtain a formal urodynamic evaluation or repeat neurology assessment to document sphincter dysfunction and baseline neurological status before intervention?
vice_opinions.public_message: Director, I agree this is a compressive cervical myelopathy with progressive deficit and sphincter involvement. The imaging-symptom match is strong, but the missing MRI details and leukocytosis give me pause. I have outlined the defensible options and my concerns. I would appreciate your decision on timing and next steps.

director_rulings.final_decision: The case requires further preoperative workup before a definitive treatment decision: high-resolution MRI of the cervical spine with foraminal views and T2 cord signal assessment, formal anesthesia airway evaluation, and evaluation of unexplained leukocytosis. Surgery is indicated in principle for progressive compressive myelopathy with sphincter involvement, but the specific approach and timing depend on these results. After workup, the department will reconvene, and the final choice between surgical decompression and a closely monitored conservative trial will be presented to the patient and family with detailed informed consent.
